The Old Testament priesthood has been fulfilled in Christ, whose single sacrifice needs no repetition (Hebrews 7:23-28; 10:11-14), so no sacrificial priestly class remains for the church.

In practice, this means you do not need a human intermediary to approach God, since you can pray, confess, and hear His Word directly through Christ. It also means your everyday service, whether at home, at work, or in your local church, is an act of priestly worship. A practical step would be to pray for your elders by name this week and ask how you can use your gifts to serve the body.

Which part of this doctrine has been on your mind? Are you wrestling with the relationship between the church's leaders and the rest of the congregation, or with the question of access to God?

question: Why is there a curse associated with hanging on a tree?
answer:
The curse comes from Deuteronomy 21:22-23: "If a man guilty of a capital offense is put to death and his body is hung on a tree, you must not leave his body on the tree overnight. Be sure to bury him that same day, for anyone who is hung on a tree is under God's curse." Hanging a executed criminal's body on a tree was a public display of shame and of God's judgment against sin. The "curse" meant that the person stood under God's righteous condemnation, and the law required that the body be buried the same day so the land God gave Israel would not be defiled.

The New Testament brings this passage to the cross. Galatians 3:13 says, "Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us, for it is written, 'Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree.'" Every human being has broken God's law (Romans 3:23), and the law pronounces a curse on that disobedience (Galatians 3:10). Jesus, who knew no sin, took that curse in our place. This is penal substitution: He bore the judgment we deserved so that we could receive the blessing of Abraham (Galatians 3:14). Peter also says that God raised Jesus, "whom you killed by hanging Him on a tree" (Acts 5:30), showing that the apostles saw the cross as the fulfillment of this very text.

The cross is therefore not a sign of God's indifference to sin but the place where His holiness and His love meet. Your guilt before God is real, and the only remedy is to turn from your sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who was cursed on the tree and raised on the third day for your forgiveness and new life. Would you like to talk about what that repentance and trust might look like for you?

question: How can we learn to trust God like the prophet Habakkuk (Habakkuk 3:17-19)?
answer:
Habakkuk did not begin with calm confidence. He began with complaint, asking how long he must cry out before God answers (Habakkuk 1:2-4). Trust grew as he brought his honest questions to God and then listened to God's answer. That is the first step for us as well: bring the raw questions to the Lord rather than hiding them behind a show of faith.

God answered him, and the answer pointed Habakkuk to His character: "the righteous will live by his faith" (Habakkuk 2:4). Paul later draws on this verse to show that justification comes by faith (Romans 1:17; Galatians 3:11), so the root of Habakkuk's trust was God's faithfulness, not his own feelings. In chapter 3, he recalls God's mighty works in the past (Habakkuk 3:2-3). Faith is strengthened as we remember who God has proven Himself to be.

Then comes the "yet" of Habakkuk 3:17-19. Figs, grapes, olives, fields, flocks, and herds all fail, and he still says, "yet I will rejoice in the LORD; I will be joyful in God my Savior" (Habakkuk 3:18). His joy does not rest on his circumstances but on the Lord Himself. This is the sanctifying work of the Holy Spirit, who forms a steady trust in us over time.

Here are some practical steps to pursue this week:

1. **Pour out your complaints honestly.** "Trust in Him at all times, O people; pour out your hearts before Him" (Psalm 62:8). Name specifically what you fear is failing, and tell God plainly what you feel.
2. **Keep a remembrance list.** Write down three specific times God was faithful to you or your family. Psalm 77:11-12 models this: "I will remember the works of the LORD; yes, I will remember Your ancient wonders. I will meditate on all Your work and consider Your mighty deeds." Review the list when fear rises.
3. **Anchor your trust at the cross.** If God "did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all," then He is able to be trusted with the smaller losses of this life (Romans 8:31-32). The One who secured your salvation by His death and resurrection will not abandon you in the valleys.

Consider sharing one of these struggles with a mature believer in your church who can pray with you and encourage you. "The prayer of a righteous person has great power" (James 5:16). Would you tell me what situation is currently testing your trust? I would be glad to walk through it with you from Scripture.

question: Why are we supposed to give thanks in everything (1 Thessalonians 5:18)?
answer:
Paul tells us to "give thanks in all circumstances, for this is God's will for you in Christ Jesus" (1 Thessalonians 5:18). Thanksgiving is not something we offer only when life goes well. It is the settled posture of people who trust that God is present, sovereign, and good in every season.

The verse does not tell us to be thankful for sin, suffering, or evil themselves, and it does not ask us to pretend that pain is pleasant. Scripture makes room for lament, as in Psalm 13:1–2, and calls us to weep with those who weep (Romans 12:15). Our thanks is directed to God, not to the hardship. We thank Him for who He is and for His promise to work all things for the good of those who love Him (Romans 8:28), even when we cannot yet see how.

The original readers were under real pressure. The Thessalonian believers faced persecution (1 Thessalonians 1:6; 3:3–4), and Paul's call to gratitude was a call to stand firm in trust. Paul practiced what he taught. He sang hymns in a Philippian prison (Acts 16:25), and he urged the church to bring every request to God "with thanksgiving," promising the peace of God that guards the heart and mind (Philippians 4:6–7).

Christians ground this gratitude in the cross. Because God gave His Son to reconcile sinners to Himself (Romans 5:8), we can thank Him even when our circumstances are hard, since our greatest need has already been met in Christ. Gratitude is also part of sanctification, the Spirit's ongoing work of making us more like Christ, and Paul prays that God would sanctify believers completely (1 Thessalonians 5:23).

For a practical step this week, choose one difficult situation and, before you bring your requests to God, write down specific things you can thank Him for about His character in that situation, such as His faithfulness, His nearness, or His past mercies. Then bring your request to Him in the light of those truths.

What circumstance is making gratitude hardest for you right now?

question: Why did Jesus refer to the temple as “my Father’s house” (John 2:16)?
answer:
Jesus called the temple "my Father's house" because He was claiming a unique relationship with the God who dwelt there, and He was acting with the authority of the Son. In John 2:13-16, Jesus came to Jerusalem for Passover, found merchants selling cattle, sheep, and doves and money changers at their tables in the temple courts, and drove them out, saying, "Do not turn My Father's house into a marketplace!" (John 2:13-16). The outer Court of the Gentiles, where non-Jews could pray, had become a noisy bazaar serving pilgrims who needed approved sacrifices and temple currency.

The phrase also draws on the Old Testament. Solomon built the temple as "a house for the Name" of the LORD (1 Kings 8:17-20), yet he confessed that heaven itself could not contain God (1 Kings 8:27). The temple was God's house because of His covenant presence there. When Jesus calls it "My Father's house," He speaks of God as His own Father in a way no other person could. The Jews understood this claim, which is why they later sought to kill Him for calling God His own Father and making Himself equal with God (John 5:17-18). This is the eternal relationship of the Father and the Son within the Trinity, and it is the basis for Jesus' authority over the house.

His disciples remembered Psalm 69:9, "Zeal for Your house consumes me" (John 2:17). When the Jews asked for a sign to justify His actions, Jesus replied, "Destroy this temple, and I will raise it again in three days" (John 2:18-19). John explains that He spoke of the temple of His body (John 2:21). Christ Himself is the true meeting place between God and humanity, which the Gospel of John makes clear when it says the Word "dwelt among us" (John 1:14). This is the incarnation, and the union of full deity and full humanity in one person is what theologians call the hypostatic union. The resurrection later confirmed this claim.

Scripture also teaches that God's people are temples of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 3:16; 1 Corinthians 6:19-20). A practical step follows: ask the Lord in prayer to show you anything in your life that has crowded out true worship, and set aside a regular time each day to read Scripture and pray, so that your life reflects a house where God is honored.

question: What does the Bible say about child abuse?
answer:
The Bible condemns child abuse in the strongest terms. It reveals a God who defends the vulnerable, and Jesus pronounced one of His most severe warnings against anyone who harms a child.

Scripture repeatedly shows God's concern for children and others who cannot protect themselves. He is "a father of the fatherless and a champion of widows" (Psalm 68:5), and He is "the helper of the fatherless" (Psalm 10:14). Israel's law commanded, "You must not mistreat any widow or fatherless child" (Exodus 22:22), and the psalmist prays that God would "defend the weak and fatherless; uphold the rights of the poor and oppressed" (Psalm 82:3).

Jesus taught with striking seriousness: "But whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in Me to stumble, it would be better for him to have a great millstone hung around his neck and be drowned in the depths of the sea" (Matthew 18:6). He also welcomed children warmly (Mark 10:13-16), showing that they are precious to Him.

Scripture also records real cases of abuse, such as Amnon's assault on Tamar (2 Samuel 13), not to approve of them but to expose the horror of sin and its lasting damage. The Bible also teaches that God sees hidden wrongs. Abel's blood "cries out to Me from the ground" (Genesis 4:10), and God brings justice in His time (Romans 12:19).

Scripture also distinguishes loving, faithful parenting from cruelty. Fathers are told, "do not exasperate your children, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord" (Ephesians 6:4). Godly authority nurtures and protects. It never crushes or harms.

If a child is in immediate danger, please call 911 (or your local emergency number) right away. You can also contact your local child protective services. Scripture calls governing authorities to restrain evil (Romans 13:4), so reporting abuse is an act of obedience and love.

If you have been hurt yourself, or you are worried about someone you know, I would gently encourage you to tell a trusted adult, and to speak with your pastor or church elders. A certified biblical counselor (ACBC) or a qualified trauma counselor can walk with you over time. God is near to the brokenhearted (Psalm 34:18), and He binds up wounds (Psalm 147:3). Would you like to share more about what is on your heart, or how I can help you find next steps?

*I do not provide medical, legal, or psychiatric advice. Please consult qualified professionals for those needs.*

question: What is Christianophobia?
answer:
Christianophobia is a term used to describe hostility, prejudice, or discrimination directed against Christians or the Christian faith. It is modeled on words like "Islamophobia" and "antisemitism," and it refers to a range of actions, from social exclusion and mockery to legal discrimination and violent persecution. Some use the term for the real and documented persecution of Christians in parts of the world, while others use it to describe bias against Christian believers in workplaces, media, or public life. Because "phobia" literally means fear, some critics question whether the term fits every case, and it is used in public debate in different ways.

Scripture does not promise that believers will be universally admired. Jesus warned, "If the world hates you, know that it hated Me before it hated you" (John 15:18-20), and Paul wrote, "Indeed, all who desire to live godly in Christ Jesus will be persecuted" (2 Timothy 3:12). Christians should also recognize that disagreement with Christian teaching is not automatically persecution. Believers are called to respond to hostility with patience and gentleness, "always being prepared to give an answer to everyone who asks you to give the reason for the hope that is in you, yet with gentleness and respect" (1 Peter 3:15-16), and to "love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you" (Matthew 5:44).

If this subject touches your own experience, practice that love in a concrete way this week by praying by name for a Christian who faces opposition at work, at school, or in another country, and ask your local church about ways to support persecuted believers.

question: How can I know that my future sins are forgiven?
answer:
Your question is a common and understandable one. Many believers fear that the sins they haven't committed yet might somehow fall outside God's forgiveness. Scripture answers with good news: your future sins are not a gap in Christ's saving work. You can know they are forgiven because forgiveness rests on what Christ has already done, not on how well you perform tomorrow.

Every person is a sinner in need of a Savior: "for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God" (Romans 3:23). God is holy, and His wrath against sin is real, so we could never make ourselves right with Him. But Christ, the eternal Son who became truly man, lived the perfect life we could not live, died as our substitute, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day: "that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that He was buried, and that He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures" (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). In His death, He bore the penalty we deserved, which is the heart of penal substitutionary atonement.

The Bible presents this forgiveness as a finished, once-for-all work. Christians are justified by faith, not by their own record. Having been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ (Romans 5:1). Colossians 2:13-14 says God has "forgiven us all our trespasses, having canceled the record of debt that stood against us." Hebrews 10:14 adds that "by one offering He has perfected forever those who are being sanctified." Since the cross, the question is not whether your sins are covered, but whether you are in Christ.

That leads to assurance. Your confidence does not rest on your future obedience, which will always be imperfect. It rests on God's faithfulness to His promise: "I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, so that you may know that you have eternal life" (1 John 5:13). For those in Christ, "there is now no condemnation" (Romans 8:1).

For the sins you will commit as a believer, God has given a path of ongoing fellowship: "If we confess our sins, He is faithful and righteous to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all unrighteousness" (1 John 1:9). Confession is not an attempt to earn forgiveness again. It is how a child returns to a loving Father. And when you sin, "we have an Advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the Righteous" (1 John 2:1).

If you have never repented of your sin and trusted in Jesus Christ alone for forgiveness, I urge you to do so today. Turn from your sin and trust in Him, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

As a next step, I encourage you to make confession a daily habit. Each evening, take a few minutes to name your sins honestly before God, thank Him for Christ's finished work, and ask Him to help you walk in obedience. If the fear of future sin is weighing heavily on you, consider sharing it with a mature believer or an elder in your local church, since "the prayer of a righteous person has great power" (James 5:16).

Would you tell me a little more about what is driving this worry? Is it a particular sin that keeps returning, or a general fear that you may not be truly saved?

question: Book of Malachi - Bible Survey
answer:
Malachi is the final book of the Old Testament in the Christian canon. It is a short prophetic book addressed to the restored community of Judah after the exile, most likely in the mid-fifth century BC, after the temple had been rebuilt. The name means "my messenger," drawn from Malachi 3:1, though some scholars debate whether it was a personal name or a title.

**Historical Setting**

The people had returned from Babylon and completed the temple, but their early zeal had faded. Priests offered blemished animals, the people withheld their tithes, marriages to foreign women and divorce were common, and many questioned whether God's justice was real. Malachi confronts these failures while holding out the hope of God's faithful covenant love.

**Literary Structure**

Malachi argues through a series of disputations. Each typically begins with a statement from God, then a question from the people, and then God's reply. The opening sets the theme: "I have loved you," says the LORD (Malachi 1:2). The outline is as follows:

- **Malachi 1:1-5:** God's love for Jacob over Esau
- **Malachi 1:6-2:9:** Corrupt sacrifices and unfaithful priests
- **Malachi 2:10-16:** Faithlessness in marriage and the covenant community
- **Malachi 2:17-3:5:** "Where is the God of justice?" and the coming refiner
- **Malachi 3:6-12:** Robbing God in tithes and offerings
- **Malachi 3:13-4:3:** The distinction between the righteous and the wicked on the day of the LORD
- **Malachi 4:4-6:** A closing call to remember the Law and the promise of Elijah

**Key Themes**

The book emphasizes God's unchanging faithfulness. "For I, the LORD, do not change" (Malachi 3:6) grounds the call to return: "Return to Me, and I will return to you" (Malachi 3:7). This reflects the doctrine of God's immutability and His covenant faithfulness, which is the foundation for any true repentance.

Malachi also teaches that genuine worship must be wholehearted. Offering God what costs nothing reveals a heart that despises His name (Malachi 1:6-8). Christians today can take this seriously when considering the sincerity of their worship and generosity.

**Connection to Christ**

Malachi 3:1 anticipates a messenger who prepares the way, and the New Testament identifies this figure with John the Baptist (Matthew 11:10; Mark 1:2). Malachi 4:5 speaks of Elijah coming before the day of the LORD, which Jesus applies to John (Matthew 11:14). Malachi 4:2 describes "the sun of righteousness" rising with healing in its wings, a promise the Gospel fulfills in Jesus, the true Light who brings salvation and new life.

**A Practical Step**

Read Malachi 3:6-12 slowly this week, and ask the Lord to show you any area where your giving, worship, or faithfulness in promises has become half-hearted. Then bring those specific areas before God in prayer, asking Him to renew your devotion and to give you a heart that delights in Him. If you would like, I can also suggest a short plan for reading the Minor Prophets together.

question: What are phylacteries?
answer:
Phylacteries (Greek *phylakteria*, "safeguards") were small leather boxes containing handwritten scripture passages, worn by Jewish men during morning prayer. Each box held four Old Testament texts: Exodus 13:1-10, Exodus 13:11-16, Deuteronomy 6:4-9, and Deuteronomy 11:13-21. They were bound to the forehead and to the left arm with leather straps, in obedience to commands like Deuteronomy 6:8, "Bind them as a sign on your hand and let them be symbols on your forehead."

This practice came from a literal reading of those commands, and it reflected a desire to keep God's word constantly before the mind and in the body's daily movements. Jesus addressed the religious leaders' use of phylacteries in Matthew 23:5, where He says, "They make their phylacteries broad and their tassels long," pointing out that the outward display had become a way to be seen by others. He warned against that kind of performance, calling His hearers to a faith that is genuine rather than merely visible.

For believers today, the lesson is less about the boxes themselves and more about the heart behind them. Scripture should be more than an external ornament. Try setting aside a fixed time each morning to read a passage from Deuteronomy 6 and ask God to write its truth on your heart, not only on your schedule.

question: Who are true worshipers (John 4:23)?
answer:
True worshipers are those who worship the Father in spirit and truth, that is, in a way that is inwardly alive through the Holy Spirit and shaped by the truth God has revealed in Jesus Christ.

Jesus speaks these words to a Samaritan woman at Jacob's well (John 4:5-6). She had raised the old dispute between Samaritans, who worshiped on Mount Gerizim, and Jews, who worshiped in Jerusalem (John 4:20). Jesus answers that the hour is coming, and is now here, when the location of worship will no longer be the deciding question (John 4:21-23). The word translated "true" (alethinos) means genuine or real, as opposed to an empty imitation. It describes worship that actually meets the living God, not worship that is merely ritual or merely a matter of place.

"Spirit" points to worship that is made alive by the Holy Spirit, who gives new birth and enables us to cry out to God as children (John 3:5-8; Romans 8:15-16). "Truth" points to worship that conforms to God's self-revelation. Jesus later declares, "I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me" (John 14:6). Because God is spirit (John 4:24), worship must be shaped by who He is and by the way He has made Himself known in His Son. This is why Christians worship the Father, through the Son, by the Spirit (Ephesians 2:18).

This means worship is not defined by a building, a tradition, or a feeling alone. Sincere emotion without the truth of Christ can go astray, and correct doctrine without the Spirit's life can grow cold. The Father is seeking worshipers who bring both together.

For a practical step this week, before you read Scripture, ask the Holy Spirit to open your heart to what the text says about Christ. Then respond to what you have read in prayer, offering God praise for who He is and thanks for what He has done in His Son.

question: Book of Obadiah - Bible Survey
answer:
Obadiah is the shortest book in the Old Testament, a single chapter of 21 verses. It is a prophecy of judgment against Edom, the nation descended from Esau, for its pride and its cruelty toward its brother Jacob (Israel).

The book opens with God's call against Edom: "The vision of Obadiah. This is what the Lord GOD says about Edom" (Obadiah 1:1). Its main themes are:

- **Pride judged:** Edom trusted in its mountain fortresses, but the Lord will bring it down (Obadiah 1:3-4).
- **Betrayal condemned:** Edom stood aloof, looted Jerusalem, and handed over survivors in the day of Israel's disaster (Obadiah 1:10-14).
- **The Day of the LORD:** Judgment on Edom is a sign of the coming "day of the LORD" for all nations, and God's justice reverses what people have done to others: "As you have done, it will be done to you" (Obadiah 1:15).
- **Deliverance and the kingdom:** Those who escape will be on Mount Zion, and "the kingdom will be the LORD's" (Obadiah 1:21).

Most scholars date the book after Babylon destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BC, since Obadiah 1:11-14 seems to describe that event, though some propose an earlier setting, and the matter remains debated. Obadiah's rivalry between the twin nations goes back to the birth of Jacob and Esau (Genesis 25:23), and the other prophets also speak against Edom (Jeremiah 49:7-22; Ezekiel 25:12-14).

For Christians, Obadiah shows that God sees the proud and rebukes those who rejoice over the suffering of others. Proverbs 24:17-18 gives a similar warning, so we should resist gloating over another's downfall and instead pray for mercy and justice to be shown in God's time.

question: What does it mean to gain the whole world but lose your soul?
answer:
Gaining the whole world but losing your soul means that no amount of success, wealth, or pleasure can make up for losing your true life before God. Jesus asks, "What good is it for a man to gain the whole world, yet forfeit his soul?" (Mark 8:36). The question assumes that your soul is worth more than everything the world can offer.

This saying comes right after Peter confesses that Jesus is the Christ, and Jesus begins to teach that He must suffer, die, and rise again. He then calls the crowd to deny themselves, take up their cross, and follow Him. In the Greco-Roman world, many people measured life by status, power, and possessions, and Jesus turns that measure upside down: "For whoever wants to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for Me and the gospel will save it" (Mark 8:35). The word translated "soul" (psyche) refers to the whole person, your life as a living being before God, not merely an invisible part of you. To forfeit your soul is to lose the life that matters most, your eternal standing with God.

The world promises security, status, comfort, and control. Some of these gifts are good in themselves, but they cannot pay the debt of sin or satisfy the deepest needs of the heart. Solomon, who had more than most, concluded, "Vanity of vanities! Says the Preacher. Vanity of vanities! All is vanity" (Ecclesiastes 1:2). Jesus then asks, "What can a man give in exchange for his soul?" (Mark 8:37). The honest answer is nothing. Your soul is not for sale, and no earthly treasure can buy it back.

The real problem is that "all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God" (Romans 3:23). Sin separates us from a holy God, and "the wages of sin is death" (Romans 6:23). Yet God shows His own love for us: "while we were still sinners, Christ died for us" (Romans 5:8). He was buried and raised on the third day, "according to the Scriptures" (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). Salvation is not earned by our achievements but is received "by grace through faith" (Ephesians 2:8-9).

Here is the invitation Jesus extends: turn from your sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died for you and rose again, and He will give you forgiveness and eternal life.

What part of this question is pressing on your heart as you think about your own life?

question: Why did God send the flood when He knew sin would continue after the flood?
answer:
God sent the flood because the world was full of present, deliberate wickedness that deserved judgment, not because He was surprised by what would follow. Genesis 6:5 says, "The LORD saw that the wickedness of man was great on the earth, and that every inclination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil all the time." The judgment answered that corruption. God's foreknowledge did not make the judgment unjust, because God never punishes people for sins they have not committed. He judges the sin that is actually before Him.

It can seem strange that a holy God would destroy a world He knew would sin again. But the flood shows something about the human heart. After the waters receded, God said, "Never again will I curse the ground because of man, for the inclination of man's heart is evil from his youth" (Genesis 8:21). The flood did not fix the problem. Judgment alone cannot cleanse a sinful heart, because the trouble is not only the world's behavior but the fallen nature of mankind (Romans 3:23).

The flood also reveals God's patience and mercy. Noah was "a preacher of righteousness" (2 Peter 2:5), and 1 Peter 3:20 says God "waited patiently in the days of Noah while the ark was being built." God gave decades of warning and made a way of rescue. Noah "found favor in the eyes of the LORD" (Genesis 6:8), and afterward God made a covenant never again to destroy all flesh by a flood (Genesis 9:11-17).

This points forward to the Gospel. Peter says the ark prefigured salvation: "eight persons were brought safely through the water. Corresponding to this, baptism now saves you" (1 Peter 3:20-21). Noah was saved through judgment, and Christians are saved through Christ, who bore the full judgment of God against sin on the cross and rose bodily from the grave (1 Peter 3:18). The flood is also a warning of the final judgment that Jesus will bring at His return (2 Peter 3:5-7; Matthew 24:37-39).

So God did not send the flood out of a failure to foresee the future. He judged real sin, showed patience to a generation that refused to listen, and kept faith with His promise. The same God now calls you to repent and trust in Jesus Christ, who died for sinners and rose again, so that you may be saved from the judgment to come.

As a practical next step, read Genesis 6 through 9 slowly this week, and then 1 Peter 3:18-22. Ask God in prayer to show you where your own heart needs cleansing, and consider sharing your questions with a mature believer or your local pastor. What about this passage stirs your thinking most?

question: Should a church tithe 10% of the offerings it receives?
answer:
Scripture does not command a church to give exactly 10% of its offerings, but it does call the church to faithful, generous, accountable stewardship of everything God places in its care.

Christians have historically held two views here. Some argue that the tithe is a moral principle that continues today. They point to Abraham giving a tenth to Melchizedek (Genesis 14:20), to Jesus affirming tithing before the cross (Matthew 23:23), and to the call to bring the full tithe (Malachi 3:10). The other view holds that the tithe was a specific provision of the Mosaic covenant, fulfilled in Christ, so that New Testament giving is measured by generosity, proportion, and a willing heart rather than a fixed percentage (2 Corinthians 9:7; Romans 14:5). I hold the second view. The New Testament never assigns a tithe to the church, and the earliest believers gave according to what each could afford (1 Corinthians 16:1-2). Still, a church may find 10% a helpful benchmark for planning, as long as it does not become a binding rule that burdens consciences.

What matters more is how the church uses what it receives. Its offerings support the pastors and elders who labor in the Word (1 Timothy 5:17-18), care for the needy within the body (Acts 6:1-4), advance the gospel to the nations, and maintain the ordinary life of the congregation. Paul also insisted that God's people handle money openly, so that no one can question their integrity (2 Corinthians 8:20-21).

As a practical next step, I'd encourage your elders to publish a simple annual budget that shows how giving is divided among ministry, mercy, missions, and operations. Then pray together over that plan and invite the congregation to see how their gifts are being used. Transparency tends to build trust and joyful giving.

Is your church currently deciding on a specific budget or giving policy? If so, I'd be glad to think it through with you.

question: Easter Bible reading plan
answer:
Here is a seven-day reading plan that walks through Holy Week to the resurrection, with a final day on its meaning for believers. Read each passage slowly, and if you can, read the Gospel accounts aloud in one sitting.

**Day 1: The King Comes to Jerusalem**
Read Matthew 21:1-11 and Zechariah 9:9. Jesus enters Jerusalem as the humble King the prophet foretold, and the crowd greets Him with the words of Psalm 118:26.

**Day 2: The Plot and the Anointing**
Read Matthew 26:1-16. Notice how the religious leaders plot to kill Jesus while a woman honors Him with costly devotion. Consider where your own heart stands between those two responses.

**Day 3: The Last Supper**
Read Luke 22:7-20 and 1 Corinthians 11:23-26. Jesus institutes the Lord's Supper as a remembrance of His body given and His blood poured out for the forgiveness of sins, the new covenant promised in Jeremiah 31:31-34.

**Day 4: The Cross**
Read Isaiah 53:4-6 and Matthew 27:32-56. Isaiah shows that the Servant bore our griefs and was pierced for our transgressions, which is the substitutionary atonement the Gospels display. Meditate on the fact that the Lord laid on Him "the iniquity of us all" (Isaiah 53:6), and that it was your sin He carried.

**Day 5: The Burial and the Silence**
Read John 19:38-42 and Psalm 16:8-11. The Son of God is laid in a tomb, yet the psalmist speaks of a body that will not see decay. Sit with the stillness of Holy Saturday, and let the silence point you forward to what God is about to do.

**Day 6: The Empty Tomb**
Read Matthew 28:1-10 and 1 Corinthians 15:3-8. Christ has risen bodily on the third day, as the Scriptures foretold. The resurrection confirms His victory over sin and death and His divinity, and it is the foundation of our justification and hope.

**Day 7: The Hope of Resurrection**
Read 1 Corinthians 15:12-22 and 15:50-58. Paul shows that because Christ is risen, believers are united to Him and will be raised. Since your labor in the Lord is not in vain (1 Corinthians 15:58), thank God for the hope this gives you.

**An actionable next step:** Set aside a set time each day this week, and before you read, ask the Lord to open your eyes to Christ in the passage. After each reading, write one sentence of thanks and one sentence of response, then share one of those sentences with a trusted believer or friend this weekend.

If you tell me whether you'd like a longer plan (for example, through Easter Sunday to Pentecost) or one suited to a family or small group, I can adjust it.

question: What is ignosticism? What is an ignostic?
answer:
Ignosticism is the view that the word "God" has no clear, coherent meaning, so the question of whether God exists is meaningless or unanswerable. An ignostic is someone who holds this view.

Ignostics usually argue that theists offer definitions of God that are vague, self-contradictory, or impossible to test, so the term never gets a meaning that can be discussed. The position is different from atheism, which denies that God exists, and from agnosticism, which says God's existence is unknown. An ignostic says the question itself is not yet well defined. The term is often attributed to the American Humanistic rabbi Sherwin Wine in the 1960s.

Christians would respond that God is not an empty word. Scripture presents Him as a personal, self-revealing God who makes Himself known, beginning with His name to Moses: "I AM WHO I AM" (Exodus 3:14). Paul writes that God's "invisible attributes" are "clearly seen" through creation (Romans 1:20), and Hebrews affirms that "whoever comes to God must believe that He exists and that He rewards those who seek Him" (Hebrews 11:6).

If you are exploring this question for yourself, you might read Exodus 3 and Romans 1 slowly and ask what it means that God speaks first. I would be glad to talk more about what you have been thinking.

question: What does it mean that Jesus is the Lord of the Sabbath?
answer:
Jesus is the Lord of the Sabbath because He is the divine Lord who instituted the Sabbath, and so He has authority over how it is rightly kept. When the Pharisees accused His disciples of breaking the Sabbath by picking grain, Jesus answered that "the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath" (Mark 2:28; see also Matthew 12:8; Luke 6:5).

The context shows what He was claiming. Jesus first pointed to David eating the consecrated bread in need (Mark 2:25-26; 1 Samuel 21:1-6), and to priests who work in the temple on the Sabbath without guilt (Matthew 12:5). He then said, "something greater than the temple is here" (Matthew 12:6), indicating that the one standing before them held a greater authority than the institutions the Pharisees revered. Just before this statement, Jesus gave the purpose of the day: "The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath" (Mark 2:27). The Sabbath is a gift from the Creator, given for human rest, worship, and flourishing, not a burden that binds people in legalistic obligations.

The title "Lord" carries weight here. In the Greek Old Testament, *kurios* regularly translates the divine name YHWH. The Sabbath was called "the Sabbath of the LORD your God" (Exodus 20:10), and God rested on the seventh day at creation (Genesis 2:2-3). By claiming lordship over the Sabbath, Jesus identified Himself with the LORD who gave it. The title "Son of Man" points to Daniel 7:13-14, where one like a son of man receives an everlasting dominion from the Ancient of Days. This is a strong witness to the deity of Christ, who shares the Father's authority.

Jesus also demonstrated this lordship by healing on the Sabbath (Mark 3:1-6; Luke 13:10-17), showing that the day exists for doing good and restoring life. The Sabbath pointed forward to a greater rest. The author of Hebrews says that "there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God" and that the one who enters God's rest "also rests from his own works" (Hebrews 4:9-10), which points to resting in the finished work of Christ. Colossians 2:16-17 describes Sabbath observances as "a shadow of what is to come," with "the substance" belonging to Christ.

Christians have historically differed on how the Sabbath principle applies today. Some keep the Lord's Day (Sunday) as a day of rest and worship in honor of Christ's resurrection, while others hold different views. Paul's counsel in Romans 14:5-6 is a helpful guide here: each should be fully convinced in his own mind and honor the Lord in what he does.

Whatever your practice, the heart of the matter is that Jesus, who gave rest and healing, is the one in whom weary sinners find rest. If you are carrying the burden of trying to earn God's favor, Jesus invites you to come to Him: "Come to Me, all who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest" (Matthew 11:28). This week, consider setting aside a regular day to stop your ordinary labors, worship with your local church, and reflect on how Christ's finished work gives you peace with God.

question: What does it mean that Jesus Christ conquered death?
answer:
Jesus conquered death by rising bodily from the grave on the third day, so that death no longer holds the final word over Him or over those who belong to Him. Scripture presents death as the wages of sin (Romans 6:23) and "the last enemy" (1 Corinthians 15:26), and Christ defeated it by dying in our place and then rising in victory.

Death came into the world through human sin (Romans 5:12), and it is the just consequence of our rebellion against a holy God. Because Jesus was truly God and truly man, He could bear the penalty we deserved. In penal substitutionary atonement, He took our guilt upon Himself on the cross, satisfying God's justice so that sinners could be reconciled to Him. Hebrews 2:14-15 says that through His death He "might destroy the one who holds the power of death" and free those who had lived "in slavery all their lives by their fear of death."

The resurrection confirms that the debt was paid. Death could not keep its hold on the sinless Son of God. Romans 6:9 declares, "Christ, having been raised from the dead, will never die again; death no longer has dominion over Him." Revelation 1:18 records His words: "I was dead, and behold, I am alive forever and ever. And I hold the keys of death and Hades." Because He lives, He is able to give what He has won. Paul rejoices, "Death has been swallowed up in victory... But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ" (1 Corinthians 15:54, 57).

For the believer, this victory means that death is no longer the end, that sin's guilt has been forgiven through faith alone in Christ alone, and that the body will one day be raised to life everlasting. Death remains a real enemy that we still face, but it has been stripped of its power. Our fear of death can give way to hope, since our future is secured by the One who rose.

The good news is that this victory is offered to you. Turn from your sins and trust in Jesus Christ, who died for sinners and rose again, and you will receive forgiveness and eternal life as His gift.

What has been weighing on you as you think about death and eternity?

question: What are the books of the Bible? What does it mean that the Bible is composed of different books?
answer:
The Bible contains 66 books: 39 in the Old Testament and 27 in the New Testament. Protestant Bibles, including the Berean Standard Bible, use this arrangement.

**Old Testament (39 books)**
Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, Ruth, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Esther, Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Song of Songs, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Lamentations, Ezekiel, Daniel, Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi

**New Testament (27 books)**
Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, Acts, Romans, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, 1 Thessalonians, 2 Thessalonians, 1 Timothy, 2 Timothy, Titus, Philemon, Hebrews, James, 1 Peter, 2 Peter, 1 John, 2 John, 3 John, Jude, Revelation

**What it means that the Bible is composed of different books**

The word "Bible" comes from the Greek *biblia*, meaning "books," so the Bible is best understood as a library rather than a single book. Its books were written over many centuries, by many human authors, in several languages (mostly Hebrew, with some Aramaic in Ezra and Daniel, and Greek in the New Testament), and in different literary forms, including law, narrative history, poetry, wisdom literature, prophecy, Gospel accounts, letters, and apocalyptic vision. Reading Psalms as if it were a legal code, or Revelation as if it were a news report, will lead to confusion, so we should attend to each book's genre and purpose.

Yet Christians believe the library has one divine Author. Second Timothy 3:16-17 teaches that "All Scripture is God-breathed," and Second Peter 1:20-21 explains that "no prophecy of Scripture came about by the prophet's own interpretation," because "men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit." The variety of human voices does not dilute God's word but displays His wisdom in using many authors to speak one truth.

That truth has a central focus. Jesus taught that the whole Old Testament pointed to Himself (Luke 24:27; Luke 24:44), and Hebrews 1:1-2 shows that God, who spoke "in various portions and in different ways" through the prophets, has now spoken "by His Son." The books therefore form a unified story of creation, fall, redemption, and restoration, climaxing in the death and resurrection of Christ.

**A practical step:** Begin with the Gospel of John, reading one chapter a day and asking, "What does this show me about Jesus?" Then, as you read other books, keep that Christ-centered thread in view.

question: What is the creation mandate / cultural mandate?
answer:
The **creation mandate** is God's command to humanity in Genesis 1:28 to be fruitful, multiply, fill the earth, subdue it, and rule over the creatures. The **cultural mandate** is another name for the same charge, used especially to emphasize that it calls people to develop families, work, arts, learning, and society in ways that honor God.

God gives this charge right after creating humanity in His image: "Then God blessed them, and God said to them, 'Be fruitful and multiply; fill the earth and subdue it. Rule over the fish of the sea, the birds of the air, and every creature that crawls on the ground'" (Genesis 1:28). In Genesis 2:15, the Lord places the man in the garden "to work it and keep it," which shows that this rule is exercised through faithful labor and stewardship, not domination or exploitation. Because the mandate is grounded in the image of God (Genesis 1:26-27), it applies to all people, not only to believers.

Christians widely agree on this text. Some, particularly in the Reformed tradition associated with Abraham Kuyper, prefer the term "cultural mandate" to highlight the call to build civilization for God's glory. Others prefer "creation mandate" to show that it belongs to God's original design for all humanity. Christians also differ on how much weight to give it in relation to the Great Commission (Matthew 28:18-20), though both are generally seen as complementary.

The fall did not cancel this mandate. God renewed it after the flood in Genesis 9:1-7, and Psalm 8 celebrates humanity's rule under God. The writer of Hebrews points to Jesus, the last Adam, as the one who fulfills this vision of rule (Hebrews 2:5-9).

For application, the mandate means that ordinary work, whether in a home, a classroom, a workplace, or a community, can be an act of worship. As Colossians 3:23-24 says, "Whatever you do, work at it wholeheartedly, as for the Lord and not for men." A practical next step is to consider how your current work or household responsibilities might serve others and honor God this week, and to ask Him in prayer for wisdom and diligence in them.

question: What does it mean that friendship with the world is enmity with God (James 4:4)?
answer:
James 4:4 means that a heart that gives its loyalty, affection, and pursuits to the world's values is hostile toward God, and that a person cannot be at peace with God while being devoted to what opposes Him. James says that whoever chooses to be a friend of the world makes himself an enemy of God.

The warning grows out of the surrounding passage. James 4:1-3 traces quarrels and conflicts to desires that go unmet and are pursued without asking God. James then calls his readers "adulterous people," an image the Old Testament prophets used for Israel's unfaithfulness to the Lord, who had bound Himself to her in covenant (see Hosea 3:1; Jeremiah 3:20). Divided loyalty is a form of spiritual infidelity, and God is not indifferent to it. James 4:5 adds that God jealously longs for the Spirit He has placed within us, which shows that His jealousy is an expression of His faithful love.

"The world" (Greek *kosmos*) does not mean God's creation, which He loves (John 3:16). It refers to the human system organized around pride, self-rule, and the craving for status, pleasure, and possessions apart from God. First John 2:15-17 describes the same reality: "the cravings of the flesh, the cravings of the eyes, and the pride of life" are "not from the Father but from the world." "Friendship" here means more than acquaintance. It means alignment of heart, adopting the world's goals as one's own. Jesus Himself ate with tax collectors and sinners (Luke 7:34), so Christians are not called to withdraw from people. They are called not to share the world's loves.

This verse is not a call to despair. James 4:6 immediately says that God "gives greater grace," and verses 7-10 call believers to submit to God, resist the devil, draw near to Him, and humble themselves. The remedy for divided loyalty is returning wholeheartedly to the Lord. Those who are in Christ are kept by Him (John 10:28-29), yet the apostle still warns us to take our loyalties seriously.

**A practical next step:** Choose one area where the world's influence is strongest for you, such as entertainment, money, reputation, or social media, and honestly identify what it is quietly teaching you to desire. Then pray Psalm 139:23-24 over that area, asking the Lord to search your heart, and replace one habit this week with time in His Word. If you have a mature believer you trust, ask them to pray with you about this, since "the prayer of a righteous person has great power" (James 5:16).

question: Why did God harden Pharaoh’s heart?
answer:
God hardened Pharaoh's heart in order to display His power and glory, so that His name would be proclaimed throughout the earth and Israel would be delivered. Exodus also shows that Pharaoh repeatedly hardened his own heart, so the account presents divine judgment and human responsibility together.

The text uses both descriptions. Pharaoh hardens his own heart: "But when Pharaoh saw that there was relief, he hardened his heart and would not listen to them" (Exodus 8:15). God also declares that He will harden it: "But I will harden his heart, so that he will not let the people go" (Exodus 4:21; see also Exodus 7:3; Exodus 9:12; Exodus 14:4). The Hebrew verbs used here, often *kabad* ("to be heavy") and *chazaq* ("to strengthen" or "make firm"), describe a heart that becomes unyielding. In Egypt's context, Pharaoh was regarded as a living god-king, so his refusal to submit to the Lord, the true God, was a direct challenge to divine authority.

God gives His reasons plainly. "But I have raised you up for this very purpose, that I may display My power in you, and that My name may be proclaimed in all the earth" (Exodus 9:16). The plagues also judged "all the gods of Egypt" (Exodus 12:12). Paul draws out this theme: "For the Scripture says to Pharaoh, 'For this very purpose I raised you up, to display My power in you, and to make My name known in all the earth.' So then, He has mercy on whom He wills, and He hardens whom He wills" (Romans 9:17-18). This is what theologians call judicial hardening, where God confirms in sin those who have already persistently rejected Him. Pharaoh's hardness was real and culpable, and God's sovereignty over it was real as well.

Paul also anticipates the objection that this seems unfair: "Who are you, O man, to talk back to God?" (Romans 9:20). Scripture does not give us a full account of every divine secret (Deuteronomy 29:29), but it does teach that God is holy, just, and sovereign, and that His purposes are wise even when we cannot trace them. Paul also notes that God endured Pharaoh "with great patience" (Romans 9:22), which shows that His judgment was not hasty.

Pastorally, the account should drive us toward humility and trust rather than speculation. If you sense your own heart growing hard, do not despair. God promises, "I will give them one heart, and put a new spirit within them. I will remove the heart of stone from their flesh and give them a heart of flesh" (Ezekiel 36:26). The same God who hardened Pharaoh in judgment has, in Christ, softened hearts in mercy. Take that concern to the Lord in prayer, asking Him to soften what is hard in you, and bring it to a trusted elder or mature believer who can pray with you (James 5:16).

What part of this passage is weighing on you most, the justice of God or the question of your own responsibility?

question: How should we treat our enemies according to Proverbs 25:21–22?
answer:
Proverbs 25:21-22 calls God's people to meet the practical needs of those who oppose them, answering hostility with kindness and leaving vindication to the LORD. The text says, "If your enemy is hungry, give him food to eat; if he is thirsty, give him water to drink. For you will heap burning coals on his head, and the LORD will reward you" (Proverbs 25:21-22).

In the ancient Near East, repaying enemies was the expected response, so this instruction was countercultural. The proverb does not ask you to ignore wrong or pretend it did not happen. It asks you to act for the good of the person who has harmed you, trusting God to be the judge.

The Apostle Paul quotes this passage in Romans 12:20, then adds, "Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good" (Romans 12:21). He first forbids personal vengeance, "Do not take revenge, my dear friends, but leave room for God's wrath, for it is written: 'Vengeance is Mine; I will repay,' says the Lord" (Romans 12:19). Christians therefore do not become the enforcers of their own justice. The "burning coals" image is debated. Some read it as the shame and conviction that kindness can awaken, leading to repentance. Others read it as a picture of God's judgment on the unrepentant. Either way, the believer's task is the same: do good, and do not take vengeance.

Jesus expands this teaching in Matthew 5:44-45 and Luke 6:35-36, calling His followers to love their enemies so that they reflect their Father's generosity. The deepest foundation is the gospel. "While we were still enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of His Son" (Romans 5:10). God did not wait for us to become worthy before showing mercy, and so we, who were once His enemies, now love our enemies as those who were forgiven much.

**A step to take this week:** Think of one person who has wronged you, and pray by name that God would bless them, asking Him to search your heart for any bitterness. Then do one concrete kindness for them, such as a meal, a word of encouragement, or a practical favor, and leave the outcome and the justice in God's hands. If the person's harm is ongoing or dangerous, please bring it to your pastors or elders and seek wise help, since love does not require you to remain exposed to abuse.

Is there a particular relationship where this teaching feels especially difficult right now?

question: What does the Bible say about indecision / being indecisive?
answer:
Scripture doesn't use the word "indecisive," but it speaks directly to the heart that wavers, and it calls God's people to wise, trusting, and courageous decisions. When Elijah confronted Israel, he asked, "How long will you waver between two opinions?" (1 Kings 18:21), showing that God cares about our divided hearts as well as our choices.

**Double-mindedness is a spiritual concern.** James writes that the one who doubts "is like the surf of the sea, driven and tossed by the wind," and he calls such a person "double-minded, unstable in all his ways" (James 1:6, 8). The remedy is not a perfect formula but asking God for wisdom in faith, since He "gives generously to all without reproach" (James 1:5). Indecision often grows when we seek certainty about every outcome instead of resting in God's character.

**Wisdom gathers counsel and trusts God's guidance.** Scripture urges us to "Trust in the LORD with all your heart and lean not on your own understanding; in all your ways acknowledge Him, and He will make your paths straight" (Proverbs 3:5-6). It also says, "victory is won through many advisers" (Proverbs 11:14), so seeking mature believers, pastors, or godly family members is a sign of humility, not weakness. God promises, "I will instruct you and teach you in the way you should go" (Psalm 32:8), which means He guides His children as they walk, not only at the moment of decision.

**Trust reaches into the future.** Jesus tells us not to be consumed by tomorrow: "Each day has enough trouble of its own" (Matthew 6:34). Much indecision is fear dressed up as careful thinking, and Paul's words to the Philippians speak to that fear: "Do not be anxious about anything, but in everything, through prayer and petition with thanksgiving, present your requests to God" (Philippians 4:6).

**A practical next step:** This week, take one decision you keep revisiting, name the two or three realistic options, and bring them to God in prayer by asking Him for wisdom and for peace about the choice. Then talk with one trusted, mature believer about it and set a date by which you will decide. Once you have prayed and sought counsel, make the choice and move forward, trusting that God can work through a decision that is not perfect.

Is there a particular decision weighing on you right now? I'd be glad to think it through with you and pray over it with you.

question: What does it mean that God will wipe away every tear (Revelation 21:4)?
answer:
Revelation 21:4 promises that in the new creation God Himself will personally comfort His people by removing every source of sorrow, so that "there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain." The image of God wiping away tears is one of tender, fatherly care, like a parent comforting a weeping child.

John writes this in the closing vision of Revelation (Revelation 21:1-8), where a new heaven and new earth replace the present order. The verse follows Revelation 21:3, which declares that God's dwelling is with mankind and that He will be with them as their God. The deepest comfort is not only the absence of tears but the presence of God Himself. Isaiah 25:8 anticipated this promise, where the Lord GOD wipes away tears from all faces and swallows up death forever. The former things pass away because the curse of Genesis 3 and its final enemy, death, are destroyed (1 Corinthians 15:26).

This is the consummation of redemption, the full restoration of creation. Romans 8:18-23 describes creation groaning under the curse while awaiting its liberation, and Revelation 21:4 is the answer to that groaning. Christians live in the "already and not yet" of God's kingdom: Christ's resurrection guarantees this future, yet believers still weep now. Jesus Himself wept at the tomb of Lazarus (John 11:35), showing that God does not despise our sorrow.

In practical terms, you do not need to hide your tears from God. Psalm 56:8 says He keeps record of your wanderings and collects your tears in His bottle. Name one specific sorrow to God in prayer this week, and then read Revelation 21:1-5 slowly, asking Him to strengthen your hope in that day.

Who enjoys this promise? Revelation 21:27 says that only those whose names are written in the Lamb's Book of Life will enter the new city. Sin separates us from a holy God, but Jesus Christ, who died for sinners and rose on the third day, is the way to Him (John 14:6). I invite you to repent of your sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, the crucified and risen Lord, so that you may be counted among those whose God will wipe away every tear.

What kind of sorrow are you carrying right now, if you are comfortable sharing it?

question: What is the meaning of “there but for the grace of God go I”?
answer:
The phrase means that anyone's circumstances, whether good or bad, reflect God's undeserved kindness, and that a person who avoids a fate others suffer should credit God's mercy rather than their own merit. It is an expression of humility and gratitude, acknowledging that we are not the authors of our own advantages.

The saying is traditionally attributed to the English Reformer John Bradford (c. 1510–1555), who reportedly spoke it as he watched criminals being led to execution. The attribution is widely repeated, but the earliest written evidence is later than his lifetime, so historians treat the exact origin as uncertain.

The idea is deeply biblical. Paul asks, "What do you have that you did not receive?" (1 Corinthians 4:7), and he confesses, "But by the grace of God I am what I am" (1 Corinthians 15:10). Jesus told the parable of the Pharisee and the tax collector, where the tax collector could only pray, "God, have mercy on me, a sinner" (Luke 18:13). In theological terms, this is the heart of justification by grace alone: we do not earn God's favor, and we do not even deserve the ordinary blessings we receive.

Applied to daily life, this truth should make you slower to judge others and quicker to thank God. When you see someone struggling with addiction, poverty, or a broken family, remember that the same weakness lives in your own heart, and that any difference between you is owed to God's grace. Ephesians 2:8-9 puts it plainly: "For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not from yourselves, it is the gift of God, not by works, so that no one can boast."

question: How can we walk in God’s ways (Psalm 128:1)?
answer:
We walk in God's ways by fearing the LORD, which means reverent trust that shapes our daily choices. Psalm 128:1 says, "How blessed is everyone who fears the LORD, who walks in His ways." The fear of the LORD is the root, and walking is the fruit that grows from it over a lifetime.

**God shows us His ways in His Word.** Moses told Israel, "And now, Israel, what does the LORD your God require of you? Only to fear the LORD your God, to walk in all His ways, to love Him, to serve the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul" (Deuteronomy 10:12). God's ways are revealed, not guessed at, so we learn them by reading and receiving Scripture. "Your word is a lamp for my feet and a light on my path" (Psalm 119:105).

**We cannot walk in God's ways by our own strength.** Jesus said, "Apart from Me you can do nothing" (John 15:5). Walking with God begins with being reconciled to Him through Christ, who is "the way and the truth and the life" (John 14:6). Justification by faith comes first, and sanctification, the Spirit's ongoing work of making us holy, follows. Paul writes, "Walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh" (Galatians 5:16). Those who are in Christ are "created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared in advance for us to walk in" (Ephesians 2:10).

**Walking is practical and daily.** Micah summarizes it: "He has told you, O man, what is good; and what does the LORD require of you? To act justly and to love mercy and to walk humbly with your God" (Micah 6:8). This shows up in ordinary decisions: how we speak to a difficult coworker, how we handle money, whether we forgive a family member, and whether we tell the truth when it costs us. James warns that we must be "doers of the word, and not merely hearers" (James 1:22).

**Walking is sustained in the community of believers.** The Christian life is not meant to be lived alone. "Let us consider how to spur one another on toward love and good works, not giving up meeting together" (Hebrews 10:24-25).

**A practical next step:** Choose one passage this week, such as Micah 6:8 or Psalm 128, and each morning ask the Lord in prayer to show you one specific way to walk in obedience that day. Then look for a mature believer who can pray with you and hold you accountable.

Where do you sense the greatest gap right now between knowing God's ways and actually walking in them? I would be glad to think through that with you.

question: What does the Bible say about the ice age?
answer:
The Bible never uses the term "ice age" or describes a period of widespread glaciation. It does, however, speak often of snow, hail, ice, and frost as works of God's hand, under His command and purpose.

Job describes God's control over winter's cold. He asks Job whether he has entered "the storehouses of the snow" or seen the "storehouses of the hail" (Job 38:22-23), and he says that "ice" comes from God's womb and "the frost of heaven" from His hand (Job 38:29-30). Psalm 147 celebrates the same Lord who "scatters the snow like wool" and "hurls down the hail like crumbs" (Psalm 147:16-17). These passages teach that the most severe cold is not random or outside God's rule but is a means by which He displays His power and wisdom.

Genesis 8:22 gives a promise that matters for this topic. After the Flood, God declares that "seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter" will continue as long as the earth remains. The Bible presents the climate's regular pattern as a covenant faithfulness of God toward creation, not as something that happens by chance.

Christians differ on how to fit the geological record, including any glacial periods, with the timeline of Genesis 1 through 11. Some hold a young earth view, reading the days of creation and the Flood as recent events that shaped the present landscape. Others hold an old earth view, seeing Genesis as compatible with a much longer history of the earth. Both groups affirm that God created all things and rules over them, so this is a secondary question on which faithful believers may reasonably disagree.

Whatever the timeline, the passages above call you to trust the God who holds the snow and the storehouses of hail. When a harsh winter or a difficult season arrives, you can pause and remember Job 38:22-23 and Psalm 147:16-17, then speak to the Lord in prayer, thanking Him that the same hand that governs the frost also governs your life.

question: What is the significance of the city of Nineveh in the Bible?
answer:
Nineveh was the great capital of the Assyrian Empire, a city on the Tigris River in what is now northern Iraq near modern Mosul. In Scripture it stands as a picture of worldly power and cruelty, yet it also shows that God's mercy reaches even the greatest enemies of His people when they repent.

The Bible first mentions Nineveh in Genesis 10:11, where it is linked to Nimrod's early kingdom in the land of Shinar. Over the centuries it grew into a center of imperial power that oppressed Israel and the surrounding nations. The Assyrians were known for brutal warfare, and Nineveh's wealth and military strength made it seem invulnerable.

Nineveh is best known from the book of Jonah. God commanded the prophet to "Go to the great city of Nineveh and preach against it, because its wickedness has come up before Me" (Jonah 1:2). Jonah fled in disobedience, but after his rescue from the sea he preached, and "The Ninevites believed God. They proclaimed a fast and put on sackcloth, from the greatest to the least of them" (Jonah 3:5). God "relented from the disaster He had threatened" (Jonah 3:10). The book closes with God's question: "Should I not have compassion on Nineveh, that great city?" (Jonah 4:11). Jonah reveals that God's mercy is not limited to Israel, and that His patience with sinners is a display of His own character.

Nineveh also appears in prophecies of judgment. Zephaniah 2:13 declares that God "will make Nineveh a desolation, a dry wasteland like the desert." Nahum is devoted entirely to its coming fall and ends with the words, "Nineveh is laid waste! Who will mourn for her?" (Nahum 3:7). Historically, the city fell to the Medes and Babylonians in 612 BC, fulfilling these warnings. This shows that God is both merciful and just: He spares those who turn from sin, yet He will not leave wickedness unpunished forever.

Jesus Himself pointed to Nineveh. He said, "The men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, for they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and now something greater than Jonah is here" (Matthew 12:41). Christ's words rebuke those who hear the greater message of the Son of God and still refuse to repent.

For you, Nineveh is a sobering reminder that no one is beyond the reach of God's call to repentance, and no one can presume upon His patience. If you are reading Jonah or Nahum, consider praying through Jonah 3 and asking the Lord to give you a humble and responsive heart to His Word, just as the Ninevites turned from their evil ways.

question: What is Epicureanism? What did Epicurus teach?
answer:
Epicureanism was a Greek philosophical school founded by Epicurus (341–270 BC) in Athens around 307 BC, where he taught in his garden community. Epicurus taught that the highest good is a tranquil life free from bodily pain and mental disturbance, which he called *ataraxia* (peace of mind) and *aponia* (freedom from pain).

His teaching rested on several key ideas:

- **Pleasure as the goal:** Epicurus defined pleasure mainly as the absence of pain and anxiety, not as indulgence. He valued simple food, modest living, prudence, and close friendships.
- **Materialism:** Everything, including the soul, is made of tiny atoms moving through empty space. Nothing exists beyond the physical world.
- **Freedom from the gods:** He held that the gods exist but are blessed and distant, uninvolved in human affairs, so people need not fear divine punishment.
- **Freedom from death:** Since the soul dissolves at death, Epicurus argued that "death is nothing to us," because when we exist, death is not present, and when death comes, we no longer exist.

Epicureanism was later expressed in Rome by the poet Lucretius in *On the Nature of Things*.

Scripture records a meeting between Paul and these philosophers: "Some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers began to debate with him" (Acts 17:18). When Paul spoke of God as Judge and of the resurrection of the dead (Acts 17:31; Acts 17:32), he directly confronted the Epicurean denial of divine judgment and life after death. Paul's gospel affirms that God is not distant from His creation, that He will judge the world through the risen Christ, and that Christ's resurrection is the foundation of hope (1 Corinthians 15:19-20).

Epicurus was right to see that anxiety corrodes the soul, but the Bible answers that anxiety with a different peace: "the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus" (Philippians 4:7). If you are wrestling with fear about the future, you might spend time this week reading Philippians 4:4-9 slowly and bringing your specific worries to God in prayer.

question: Book of Philippians - Bible Survey
answer:
Philippians is a letter from the apostle Paul to the church he helped plant in Philippi, a Roman colony in Macedonia. He most likely wrote it from prison, traditionally dated to Rome around AD 60–62, and its central theme is joy in Christ that endures through suffering.

**Background**
Paul founded this church on his second missionary journey, when Lydia, a seller of purple cloth, believed and the Philippian jailer was converted (Acts 16:11-40). The church had sent a gift to Paul through Epaphroditus, who had nearly died in the work, and Paul sends this letter back with him (Philippians 2:25-30; Philippians 4:18).

**Key Themes**
- **Joy in suffering:** Paul writes, "Rejoice in the Lord always; again I will say, Rejoice!" (Philippians 4:4), even while chained.
- **The humility and exaltation of Christ:** The hymn in Philippians 2:5-11 describes the incarnation, in which the eternal Son took the form of a servant while remaining truly God, and His exaltation as Lord.
- **Justification by faith:** Paul rejects self-earned righteousness and embraces "the righteousness from God based on faith" (Philippians 3:9).
- **Unity in the gospel:** Believers are to "stand firm in one spirit, with one mind striving together for the faith of the gospel" (Philippians 1:27).
- **Contentment in Christ:** Paul has learned to be content in every circumstance through Christ who strengthens him (Philippians 4:11-13).

**Outline**
1. Greeting and thanksgiving (Philippians 1:1-11)
2. Paul's circumstances and his life in Christ (Philippians 1:12-30)
3. Humility and unity modeled by Christ, Timothy, and Epaphroditus (Philippians 2:1-30)
4. Warning against false teaching and pressing on toward the goal (Philippians 3:1-21)
5. Final exhortations, thanks, and greetings (Philippians 4:1-23)

**Significance for Today**
Philippians shows that believers can rejoice in the Lord even when circumstances are hard, because their security rests in Christ rather than in their situation. For a practical step, the next time you feel anxious, bring your specific requests to God in prayer with thanksgiving, as Paul instructs in Philippians 4:6-7, and let His peace guard your heart.

question: In what ways was Moses like Jesus?
answer:
Moses was a type of Christ, a real historical figure whose life and ministry foreshadowed the greater work of Jesus. The clearest link is the promise that God would raise up a prophet like Moses: "I will raise up for them a Prophet like you from among their brothers. I will put My words in His mouth, and He will tell them everything I command Him" (Deuteronomy 18:15-18). Peter applies this directly to Jesus (Acts 3:22-23).

Several other parallels show this pattern:

- **Deliverance from a murderous decree:** Pharaoh ordered the Hebrew sons killed, and Moses was preserved (Exodus 1:22-2:10). Herod later ordered the infants of Bethlehem killed, and Jesus was carried to Egypt and preserved (Matthew 2:13-18).
- **Mediator of a covenant:** Moses sprinkled blood and ratified the covenant at Sinai (Exodus 24:3-8). Jesus, the mediator of a better covenant, inaugurated the new covenant by His own blood (Luke 22:20; Hebrews 9:15).
- **Forty days on the mountain:** Moses fasted forty days and nights while receiving the law (Exodus 34:28). Jesus fasted forty days in the wilderness before beginning His ministry (Matthew 4:1-2).
- **Testing in the wilderness:** Israel was tested for forty years, and Moses reminded them of that trial (Deuteronomy 8:2-3). Jesus, the true Israel, was tested for forty days and answered each temptation with Scripture (Matthew 4:3-11).
- **Giver of instruction from a mountain:** Moses delivered the law from Sinai (Exodus 19-20). Jesus taught the true meaning of the law from a mountainside (Matthew 5:1-2).
- **Intercessor for the people:** Moses pleaded with God to spare Israel after the golden calf (Exodus 32:11-14). Christ now lives to intercede for His people (Hebrews 7:25).
- **Shared glory with heaven:** Moses appeared with Jesus at the transfiguration, speaking of Jesus' "departure" (Greek *exodos*) that He would accomplish in Jerusalem (Matthew 17:1-3; Luke 9:30-31).

The New Testament also shows where Christ is greater. Moses was a faithful servant in God's house, but Christ is the faithful Son over that house (Hebrews 3:5-6). The law came through Moses, but grace and truth came through Jesus Christ (John 1:17). Moses could not enter the Promised Land because of his own sin at Meribah (Numbers 20:12), while Jesus is the sinless high priest who was tempted yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15). Moses pointed to the law that exposes sin, while Jesus accomplished the atonement that removes it.

This is what theologians call typology: God displays His redemptive pattern in earlier history, and it reaches its fulfillment in Christ. The Christian application is to read the Pentateuch with expectation, looking for the Savior who fulfills what Moses could only foreshadow. A practical next step would be to read Deuteronomy 18 and Hebrews 3 together this week, noting how the author of Hebrews shows Christ as both like and greater than Moses.

question: What is Socinianism?
answer:
Socinianism was a 16th and 17th century anti-Trinitarian movement named after Faustus Socinus (1539-1604), an Italian theologian whose views shaped the Polish Brethren and later Unitarian thought. It denied the eternal deity of Christ, the Trinity, and the traditional doctrine of the atonement, and it is outside the historic orthodox faith.

Socinians taught that Jesus was a human being, uniquely born of the Virgin Mary and empowered by God, but not eternally God the Son. They understood Christ's death primarily as a moral example and a revelation of God's love, rather than as a substitutionary sacrifice that satisfied God's justice for sinners. They also tended to rely heavily on human reason in interpreting Scripture, which led them to set aside texts that affirm Christ's divinity.

The historic church rejected these views because Scripture clearly teaches that the Word "was God" (John 1:1) and that "in Christ all the fullness of the Deity lives in bodily form" (Colossians 2:9). The Bible also presents Christ's death as a real atoning sacrifice: "God demonstrates His own love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us" (Romans 5:8), and "He made Him who had no sin to be sin for us, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God" (2 Corinthians 5:21). If Jesus were merely human, He could not be the one mediator "between God and mankind" (1 Timothy 2:5).

For a believer, the practical weight of this is that our hope rests on who Christ is and what He has done. The Son who is truly God and truly man is the one who saves, so it is worth examining any teaching about Him closely against the whole of Scripture.

question: Can an unmarried man be a deacon or elder?
answer:
Scripture does not explicitly require an elder or deacon to be married, but many faithful churches have historically expected it, so this is a question on which Christians sincerely differ. The qualifications appear in 1 Timothy 3:1-13 and Titus 1:6-9, where Paul writes that an overseer must be "the husband of one wife" (1 Timothy 3:2; see also 1 Timothy 3:12 for deacons).

The strongest case for requiring marriage is that Paul's wording assumes a man who is, or has been, a husband, and that the following verses, "he must manage his own household well" (1 Timothy 3:4), point to a man already leading a family. On this reading, an unmarried man would lack the household experience Paul seems to expect.

I hold that an unmarried man is not automatically disqualified. The phrase "husband of one wife" most naturally addresses marital faithfulness, ruling out polygamy, adultery, and a pattern of unfaithfulness, rather than setting marriage itself as a requirement. Paul also commends singleness as a gift that allows undivided devotion to the Lord (1 Corinthians 7:7-8, 32-35), and he himself was unmarried. The household qualification is better understood as a test of a man's ability to shepherd people with patience and wisdom, which a single man can demonstrate in other settings. That said, the local church should weigh each man's character, self-control, and proven ability to lead, and it is wise for a congregation to be cautious and prudent in such cases.

If you are asking because of a situation in your own church, I would encourage you to talk with your elders and pastors, who can help you apply these texts to your particular context. Is this a question you are considering for yourself, or for your congregation?

question: Is it better, spiritually, to be poor than to be rich?
answer:
Scripture does not say poverty is holier than wealth, and it does not call riches sinful in themselves. The spiritual question is where the heart rests. The Bible warns that both poverty and riches carry their own temptations, and that the love of money is the real danger.

Agur's prayer in Proverbs 30:8-9 captures this balance. He asks God for neither poverty nor riches, fearing that wealth could make him forget the Lord and that want could drive him to dishonesty. Jesus similarly blesses the poor in spirit (Matthew 5:3) and the poor who wait on God (Luke 6:20), but He also warns that it is hard for the rich to enter the kingdom of God (Mark 10:23-25). Yet Abraham (Genesis 13:2) and Joseph of Arimathea (Matthew 27:57) were wealthy men whom Scripture honors as godly. The point is not the amount of money but the posture of the heart.

Paul locates the danger precisely: "the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil" (1 Timothy 6:10). Money becomes an idol when we trust it, measure our worth by it, or cling to it instead of God (Colossians 3:5). This is why Paul instructs wealthy believers not to put their hope in uncertain riches but in God, and to be rich in good works (1 Timothy 6:17-18). Meanwhile, James reminds us that God has chosen many who are poor in the world to be rich in faith (James 2:5), so material lack is no barrier to spiritual maturity.

The mark of spiritual health in either situation is contentment, which Paul learned through every circumstance (Philippians 4:11-13). Contentment is the fruit of sanctification, the Spirit's ongoing work of making us more like Christ, and it grows as we trust that the Lord who provides is also the Lord who sustains.

For a practical step, consider reviewing your last month of spending and giving.
