The universal church is the whole company of true believers in Christ across all times and places, while a local church is a particular congregation of believers who gather in one place for worship, teaching, and fellowship. Both belong to the same Lord, but they differ in scope and function.

**The Universal Church**
The universal church includes every person redeemed by Christ through faith, from Pentecost until His return, along with the saints who have gone before. Paul describes Christ as head "over all things to the church, which is His body, the fullness of Him who fills all in all" (Ephesians 1:22-23). Jesus promised, "I will build My church, and the gates of Hades will not overcome it" (Matthew 16:18). The writer to the Hebrews speaks of a gathering of the firstborn whose names are written in heaven (Hebrews 12:22-23). This church is not a building or denomination. Because God alone sees the heart, its full membership is known only to Him, which is why it is sometimes called the "invisible" church.

**The Local Church**
A local church is a visible congregation of baptized believers who meet under the preached Word, celebrate the ordinances, and are shepherded by recognized leaders. The New Testament speaks of "the church of God in Corinth" (1 Corinthians 1:2) and describes elders appointed for the churches in various cities (Acts 14:23). In the local church, Christians practice the "one another" commands, are discipled, and exercise church discipline when needed (Hebrews 10:24-25; Matthew 18:15-17).

**How They Relate**
The local church is not a lesser or optional version of the universal church. It is where the universal body becomes visible in a particular place. Believers in every congregation share one faith and one Lord, so their unity reaches beyond their own walls, and that unity is lived out concretely in a specific community.

Christians differ on how local churches should be governed. Many Reformed Baptists, for example, hold to elder-led congregational government with local autonomy, while Presbyterians, Anglicans, and others hold different structures. These are secondary matters on which faithful believers may disagree, and the essential point is that every believer belongs to a local body.

**A Practical Step**
If you are a believer not yet committed to a local church, make it a priority this month. Visit a congregation that preaches the gospel faithfully, meet the pastors, and ask how you can serve and be known. Scripture pictures no solitary Christian, but a body in which every member is needed (1 Corinthians 12:12-27).

Is there a particular situation, such as moving, church hurt, or uncertainty about where to belong, that prompted your question?

question: Why should I believe in God?
answer:
You may have good reasons to doubt. Many people wonder whether belief in God is only wishful thinking, or whether science has made Him unnecessary. Those are honest questions, and Christians believe they deserve careful answers. Belief in God is reasonable because the evidence points to Him, and the Bible explains why.

The first reason is creation. The universe had a beginning, and it is ordered, intelligible, and fine-tuned for life. Science tells us how things work, but it does not tell us why there is anything at all. Psalm 19:1 says, "The heavens declare the glory of God; the skies proclaim the work of His hands." Romans 1:20 teaches that God's "invisible attributes, that is, His eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly seen, being understood from what has been made." The world does not prove God the way a math equation does, but it points toward a Creator.

The second reason is the moral law within us. Most people sense that some things are truly right and wrong, such as cruelty, betrayal, and injustice, and we feel guilt when we violate that sense. Romans 2:15 says the work of the law is "written on their hearts, their consciences also bearing witness." Our moral conscience is hard to explain if we are only accidents of matter. It makes more sense if we were made by a holy and righteous God.

The third reason is the ache in the human heart. Ecclesiastes 3:11 says God "has set eternity in the hearts of men." Many people feel a longing for something beyond this world, and nothing in this world fully satisfies it. Augustine captured this when he wrote that our hearts are restless until they rest in God.

Finally, there is the testimony of Jesus Christ. The Gospels record His claims, His miracles, and His resurrection from the dead. Paul appeals to eyewitnesses in 1 Corinthians 15:3-8, noting that Christ appeared to more than five hundred people, many of whom were still living when he wrote. The resurrection is the central claim of the Christian faith, and if it happened, it confirms everything Jesus said about Himself.

Here is the heart of the matter. The Bible teaches that every person has sinned against God and fallen short of His holy standard (Romans 3:23). That sin separates us from Him, and we cannot fix it by our own effort. But God, who is rich in mercy, loved us while we were still sinners. Romans 5:8 says, "God demonstrates His own love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us." Jesus, who is truly God and truly man, lived a perfect life, bore the penalty for our sin on the cross, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). He now reigns as Lord.

Salvation is not earned. Ephesians 2:8-9 says, "For by grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not from yourselves, it is the gift of God, not by works, so that no one can boast." So I would gently invite you to turn from your sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

What part of this feels most difficult for you to believe, and what has led you to ask the question?

question: How is the church the Body of Christ?
answer:
The church is the Body of Christ because every believer is united to Jesus, who is the living Head, and by the Holy Spirit we are joined together into one organism through which Christ lives, speaks, and serves in the world. Paul calls the church Christ's body because the relationship is both spiritual and organic, not merely an organization or a gathering of like-minded people.

**Christ is the Head.** Scripture describes Christ as the one who rules over His people. Paul writes that God "appointed Him as head over all things for the church, which is His body, the fullness of Him who fills all in all" (Ephesians 1:22-23). Colossians 1:18 adds that "He is the head of the body, the church." Headship means authority, life, and direction flow from Christ to His people (Ephesians 4:15-16).

**The Spirit forms the body.** Believers do not become members of this body by their own effort. "For we were all baptized by one Spirit into one body, whether Jews or Greeks, slaves or free, and we were all given the one Spirit to drink" (1 Corinthians 12:13). This baptism by the Spirit refers to our union with Christ at conversion, and it makes diverse people one body in Him.

**Members belong to one another.** Because we share one life, we are interdependent. "Now you are the body of Christ, and each one of you is a part of it" (1 Corinthians 12:27). Paul insists that no member can say to another, "I don't need you" (1 Corinthians 12:21), and that when one part suffers, all suffer together (1 Corinthians 12:26). Each believer receives gifts from the Spirit for the good of the whole (Romans 12:4-8).

**Application:** If you are a believer, your faith is not meant to be lived alone. Commit yourself to a local church where the Word is faithfully preached and the sacraments are rightly administered, and ask the elders how you might serve using the gifts God has given you. Christ's body grows as each member does its part in love (Ephesians 4:16).

question: What are some undeniable examples of divine intervention?
answer:
The Bible records many occasions when God acted directly and visibly in history, and Christians receive these accounts as real events, not symbolic stories. Among the clearest are these:

- **The plagues and the parting of the Red Sea:** God judged Egypt and then divided the waters so Israel could pass on dry ground (Exodus 14:21-22). The whole nation witnessed it, and Moses later sang of it as the Lord's saving act (Exodus 15:1-2).
- **Elijah on Mount Carmel:** Before the prophets of Baal, the Lord sent fire from heaven that consumed a sacrifice soaked with water, and the people fell on their faces and confessed, "The LORD, He is God!" (1 Kings 18:38-39).
- **The fiery furnace:** Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego walked unharmed in the flames, and the king saw a fourth figure with them (Daniel 3:24-25).
- **Daniel in the lions' den:** God sent His angel and shut the lions' mouths, and Daniel came out without a scratch because he trusted his God (Daniel 6:22-23).
- **Peter's escape from prison:** An angel led Peter past the guards and through the iron gate while the church prayed (Acts 12:6-11).

The greatest intervention, and the foundation of the Christian faith, is the bodily resurrection of Jesus Christ. Paul appeals to eyewitnesses, including more than five hundred people at one time, many of whom were still living when he wrote (1 Corinthians 15:3-8). He also declares that if Christ has not been raised, faith is empty (1 Corinthians 15:14, 17). The resurrection shows that Jesus is the Son of God "with power" (Romans 1:4).

Some people find such accounts hard to believe, perhaps because they seem too extraordinary or because they doubt God acts in the world today. Christians believe the God who created all things is not limited by the laws of nature He established, and that His purposes are wise even when His works astonish us.

If the risen Christ is real, He calls every person to respond. Turn from your sin and trust in Jesus Christ, who died for sinners and rose on the third day, for forgiveness and new life.

As a next step, read Acts 2 this week and notice how Peter pointed to the resurrection as the proof that the crucified Jesus is Lord and Christ (Acts 2:22-24, 32-36). Which of these accounts has most stirred your thinking?

question: What is the institutional church?
answer:
The institutional church is the church viewed as a visible, organized body, with recognizable structures such as membership, leadership, worship gatherings, creeds, and the ordinances of baptism and the Lord's Supper. Sociologists and historians often use the term for formal church structures and denominations, while Christians use it to describe the visible church, as distinct from the invisible church, the whole company of the redeemed that is fully known only to God.

Scripture presents the church as both a living fellowship and an ordered body. Christ promises to build His church (Matthew 16:18), elders and deacons are appointed to oversee and serve (1 Timothy 3:1-7; Acts 14:23), and believers are commanded not to neglect meeting together (Hebrews 10:24-25). The Reformed tradition affirms the church's visible form as God's design, with Christ as its sole head ruling through His Word and Spirit. Structures exist to serve the church's life, not to replace it, so a faithful institution is one that stays submitted to Scripture.

Some people hear "institutional" as a criticism, suggesting bureaucracy or lifeless routine, and that concern is sometimes justified when churches drift from the Bible. Yet the answer to abuse is reform, not abandoning the gathered, ordered life of the church.

If you are a believer not yet committed to a local congregation, consider visiting a church that preaches the Bible faithfully, administers baptism and the Lord's Supper, and has qualified elders. Ask the pastor how membership works there, and begin attending regularly so you can grow in fellowship and service.

question: Is Christianity true?
answer:
Yes, Christianity is true, because it rests on a historical event: Jesus Christ died for sinners and rose bodily from the dead on the third day. The apostle Paul put it plainly: "if Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain" (1 Corinthians 15:14).

You may wonder whether a religion this old can be trusted, or whether a loving God could allow so much suffering. Others find it hard to believe that Jesus is the only way to God. These are serious questions, and Christians take them seriously.

The resurrection is not a story passed down with no witnesses. Paul wrote within about 25 years of the cross and recorded an earlier creed he had received, which says Christ "appeared to Cephas, then to the Twelve. After that, He appeared to more than five hundred brothers at one time, most of whom are still alive, though some have fallen asleep" (1 Corinthians 15:5-6). Paul invited his readers to check these witnesses for themselves. Eyewitnesses, including skeptics like James, the brother of Jesus, became willing to die for this testimony (1 Corinthians 15:7; John 20:28).

The Bible also explains why we need a Savior. God is holy and just, and "all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God" (Romans 3:23). Sin separates us from Him, and "the wages of sin is death" (Romans 6:23). God's justice is real, but so is His love. In penal substitution, Christ took the punishment our sins deserved: "Christ died for sins once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God" (1 Peter 3:18). He was buried, raised on the third day, and now reigns as Lord. That is the good news.

Justification means we are declared righteous before God, not by our own effort, but by grace through faith. "For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not from works, so that no one can boast" (Ephesians 2:8-9).

So I would lovingly invite you to repent, that is, turn from your sin, and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose again for you. "Repent, then, and turn back, so that your sins may be wiped out" (Acts 3:19). Jesus is the only Mediator between God and man (1 Timothy 2:5), and "there is salvation in no one else" (Acts 4:12).

As a next step, I encourage you to read John 20 and 1 Corinthians 15 slowly and see the evidence for yourself. What part of this feels most difficult to accept, or what led you to ask this question?

question: What is ministry?
answer:
Ministry is service done for God and for others, carried out in the name and strength of Christ. The English word comes from the Latin *ministerium*, and the New Testament word *diakonia* means service or waiting on someone.

Jesus defined ministry by His own life: "For even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many" (Mark 10:45). Ministry therefore is not mainly about status or achievement. It is following the Servant King in humble love.

Scripture describes ministry in two related senses:

- **Every believer's ministry:** Each Christian has received gifts from the Holy Spirit and is called to use them for the good of others. "As each one has received a gift, use it to serve one another as faithful stewards of God's grace in its various forms" (1 Peter 4:10). This is sometimes called the priesthood of all believers, grounded in the truth that all who are united to Christ have access to God and a share in His work.
- **Church leadership ministry:** Christ gave specific leaders, including pastors and teachers, "to equip the saints for the work of ministry, to build up the body of Christ" (Ephesians 4:11-12). Their role is to shepherd, teach, and guard the flock, while the whole congregation serves together.

In practice, ministry may look like teaching a child a Bible story, visiting someone who is sick, or faithfully doing your job with integrity as an act of worship. Consider this week how God has gifted you, and ask Him to show you one specific place in your home, church, or workplace where you can serve someone in His name.

What area of service are you currently thinking about, or what has led you to ask this question?

question: What is classical apologetics?
answer:
Classical apologetics is a method of defending the Christian faith that begins by establishing the existence of the God of Scripture through rational argument, and then shows that Christianity is historically credible, especially in the resurrection of Jesus Christ. Its best-known practitioners include Thomas Aquinas in the medieval period and, in more recent generations, R.C. Sproul, William Lane Craig, and others who argue for "classical theism" alongside historical evidence.

The approach typically moves in two stages. First, it argues from reason and creation (drawing on Romans 1:19-20, which says God's invisible attributes are clearly seen through what has been made) to the reality of a necessary, uncaused, personal First Cause. Arguments such as the cosmological argument (that the universe had a beginning and therefore a cause), the teleological argument (that the order of nature points to design), and the moral argument (that objective moral law implies a moral Lawgiver) belong here. Second, it turns to the historical claims of Christianity, examining evidence for Jesus' death, the empty tomb, and the appearances of the risen Christ, as recorded in 1 Corinthians 15:3-8, to show that the Gospel is grounded in real events rather than myth.

Classical apologetics differs from presuppositional apologetics, associated with Cornelius Van Til, which holds that the Christian worldview must be assumed from the start because all reasoning depends on God. Classical apologists generally view natural reason as a genuine, though limited and fallen, pathway that can prepare the way for the gospel. Many Christians find both approaches helpful, and they share a common goal: giving a reason for the hope within us with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15).

question: Why does God allow birth defects?
answer:
Questions like this often come from real heartache, whether from a child you love, a pregnancy that brought fear instead of joy, or a long struggle to reconcile a good God with a world that hurts its most vulnerable members.

Scripture teaches that God made the world "very good" (Genesis 1:31), but sin brought disorder into creation. When Adam fell, death and decay entered the world (Romans 5:12), and the whole creation was subjected to futility (Romans 8:20; Genesis 3:17-19). Birth defects are part of that broken world, not part of God's original design. Because God is holy, He is not the author of sin or evil, yet He remains sovereign over all that happens. He is never surprised, and He is never without purpose.

We should also be careful not to assume that every affliction is a direct punishment for a specific sin. When His disciples asked whether a man's blindness was due to his own sin or his parents' sin, Jesus answered that neither was the cause, but that "the works of God might be displayed in him" (John 9:1-3). God's sovereign purposes can be far larger than we can see. As He reminded Job, His wisdom is beyond our full comprehension (Job 38:4; Job 42:2-3).

Honesty matters here. Scripture does not give a detailed explanation for every individual case, and we should not pretend to know more than God has revealed. What He has revealed is His character and His promises. Romans 8:28 assures believers that God works all things together for good for those who love Him, and that good is ultimately conformity to Christ, not a life free from pain. The Gospel also shows that God did not remain distant from suffering. In Christ, He took on human flesh and "bore our griefs and carried our sorrows" (Isaiah 53:3-5). The resurrection promises a day when the broken order will be made new. God will "wipe away every tear," and there will be "no more death or mourning or crying or pain" (Revelation 21:4). Believers look forward to a transformed body, conformed to the body of Christ's glory (Philippians 3:21).

For a next step, bring this question honestly to God in prayer. The Psalms give you words for that, especially Psalm 13 and Psalm 22, where the psalmists cry out with confusion and still trust the Lord. If this affects your family or a child in your care, ask a pastor or mature believer in your church to walk alongside you, since "the prayer of a righteous person has great power" (James 5:16).

Would you like to share more about what has prompted this question? I would be glad to think through it with you.

question: Why doesn't God heal everyone?
answer:
Your question touches one of the most painful experiences a person can have, whether you are praying for a body that is failing, a child who is sick, or a loved one who is suffering. Scripture does not hide that struggle.

God is able to heal, and He sometimes does so in ways that display His power. Yet the Bible does not promise that every sickness will be healed in this present age. Christians have long understood several truths that help us think about this.

First, we live in a world marred by sin. Paul writes that "the whole creation has been groaning together" (Romans 8:22), and that we ourselves "groan inwardly as we eagerly wait for adoption, the redemption of our bodies" (Romans 8:23). Sickness and death are the fruit of the fall (Genesis 3:17-19), and our bodies have not yet been fully restored.

Second, God's purposes are wiser than our understanding. When Jesus was asked about a man born blind, He answered, "Neither this man nor his parents sinned, but that the works of God might be displayed in him" (John 9:3). Job, who lost nearly everything, was answered not with a full explanation but with a revelation of God's wisdom and sovereignty (Job 38-42). We are not always given the reasons, but we are given the Lord Himself.

Third, God can give grace within weakness. Paul pleaded three times for his affliction to be removed, and the Lord answered, "My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness" (2 Corinthians 12:9). Some believers are healed in body, and others are sustained in suffering. Both can be the work of a faithful God.

Finally, the final healing is certain. Christ bore our sicknesses and wounds on the cross (Isaiah 53:4-5; Matthew 8:16-17), and He rose bodily from the dead as the firstfruits of the resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:20-23). One day, "He will wipe away every tear from their eyes. There will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain" (Revelation 21:4). Every healing we see now is a foretaste of that day.

Because the healing of our bodies is bound up with the resurrection, I would gently ask you to consider Jesus Christ. Repent of your sin and trust in Him, who died for you and rose again, and you will find forgiveness and the living hope of a body made new.

As a next step, I encourage you to bring your specific request before the Lord in honest prayer, using the language of Psalm 13 or Psalm 62:8, and to ask your church elders to pray with you and anoint you as James 5:14-16 describes. The Lord welcomes raw honesty.

Who is the person you are praying for, and what has been most difficult for you to trust God with?

question: What does it mean that the Bible is self-authenticating?
answer:
The Bible is self-authenticating in that its divine authority rests on God, who speaks in it, rather than on any human court, church, or external proof that must first certify it. Scripture is the Word of God, and it bears its own testimony to that truth.

The Reformed tradition expresses this in the Westminster Confession of Faith (1.5), which says that the authority of Scripture "dependeth not upon the testimony of any man or church, but wholly upon God (who is truth itself), the author thereof." John Calvin made a similar point in his *Institutes* (1.7), arguing that Scripture is established by the inward testimony of the Holy Spirit and not by human argument alone. Calvin also taught that the Spirit's testimony does not add new revelation. It enables believers to recognize the voice of the One who has already spoken.

Scripture teaches this throughout. Paul says that "all Scripture is God-breathed" (2 Timothy 3:16), so its origin is divine. Peter says that "prophecy never had its origin in the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit" (2 Peter 1:20-21). Jesus says that "My sheep hear My voice, and I know them, and they follow Me" (John 10:27), which shows that God's people recognize His voice. Paul adds that "the natural man does not accept the things of the Spirit of God" but that these things "are discerned by the Spirit" (1 Corinthians 2:14).

Christians have understood the matter in a few different ways:

- **The church-authority view** (Roman Catholic): the church's recognition of the canon is what gives Scripture its authority. Catholics regard the church's teaching office as the living interpreter of Scripture and the authority that identifies it.
- **The evidentialist view** (common in classical apologetics): reasoned arguments for the Bible's reliability, such as historical evidence, prophecy, and the resurrection, establish that Scripture is trustworthy before it is received as God's Word.
- **The self-authenticating view** (Reformed): Scripture is the final authority, the one that judges all other claims. External evidence can confirm and illustrate its truth, but the Spirit's testimony to the Word is what brings the believer to certainty.

I hold the third view. It guards against placing the Bible under the judgment of human institutions, and it also accounts for the fact that people who have never studied apologetics can know God's voice in Scripture. It does not make Scripture unaccountable, though. Its claims can be tested against the text, and they consistently hold up to examination.

For practical application, if you are unsure about Scripture's authority, don't start by trying to prove the Bible from outside it. Read a book such as John or Romans, ask the Lord to open your eyes as Psalm 119:18 asks, and notice how the text speaks to your conscience and your need for Christ. You might also ask a mature believer in your church to read through a passage with you, since "faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ" (Romans 10:17).

What led you to ask about this? Are you wrestling with the Bible's authority, or looking to explain it to someone else?
